metaDescription: Seven electric coffee grinders compared on blade versus burr design, step counts, retention, static and noise, from simple blade units to a Baratza.
expertTake: The Baratza Encore is the coffee grinder to buy if you brew every day and want a repairable burr grinder with consistent particles, and the OXO Brew conical burr is the pick for easy daily use with a memory dial. Skip blade grinders for espresso and pour-over, because blades chop unevenly and only grind time sets the size.
introParagraphs: A coffee grinder turns whole beans into the particles your brewer needs. Even particles extract evenly, while a mix of dust and chunks gives a brew that is both bitter and sour. That is why grind quality matters more than the brewer for many people.

The big divide is blade versus burr. Blades chop beans with a spinning propeller, while burrs crush them between two surfaces at a set gap. Step counts, retention, static and noise add detail. The seven grinders below span both designs and are judged on how they behave over a year of daily use.

products.name: Baratza Encore ZCG485 Conical Burr Coffee Grinder
products.description:
The Encore uses 40 millimetre conical steel burrs driven by a motor that Baratza describes as powerful, with a front-mounted pulse button and a simple on/off switch. It is the brand's best-selling entry grinder and has a small footprint.

Conical burrs crush beans between two cones, which produces fairly even particles and runs cooler than a fast blade. Compared with the OXO in this guide it has a simpler control set and a reputation for easy repair, while the OXO adds a memory dial and a built-in timer.

Baratza sells replacement burrs and parts, which is the real ownership benefit for a grinder used daily. Brush out the chute weekly and avoid water on the burrs. Because it is a simple machine, most repairs involve a screwdriver and a replacement part rather than a service visit.
products.bestFor: Daily brewers who want a repairable burr grinder with consistent particles.
pros: Parts and burrs are sold for repair
Front pulse button is easy to use
cons: Fine espresso needs a pricier grinder

products.name: OXO Brew Conical Burr Electric Grinder, 12 oz Hopper
products.description:
The OXO Brew has 40 millimetre stainless conical burrs, fifteen grind settings plus 43 micro-adjustments and a one-touch start that remembers your last setting. A twelve ounce hopper holds a good supply of beans.

The micro-adjustments are what separate it from simpler grinders. Step count and range are different things, so 15 steps with micro-adjustments can cover more of the useful drip to espresso-adjacent range than 40 coarse clicks. Compared with the Baratza it adds a timer feel and convenience, and compared with the Cuisinart it uses conical burrs.

Brush out the chute weekly, keep the hopper dry and store beans in an airtight container. The large hopper is handy for a bag at a time, but it also exposes beans to air, so keep it covered and fill it only as needed.
products.bestFor: Daily brewers who want a memory setting and a large hopper.
pros: One-touch start remembers the last setting
12 oz hopper holds a full bag
cons: Retention in the chute needs brushing
Costs more than basic burr grinders

products.name: Cuisinart Supreme Grind DBM-8P1 Flat Burr Coffee Grinder
products.description:
The DBM-8P1 uses stainless steel flat burrs with eighteen grind settings, and the listing says its uniform particles help even extraction. A safety interlock stops the motor when the hopper is removed.

Flat burrs are a step up from blades without a commercial price, and they tend to give a sharp particle distribution. Compared with the Baratza's conical burrs it runs a faster motor and produces somewhat more heat and noise, while compared with the SHARDOR it is a longer-established design.

The settings cluster toward coarser sizes, so espresso needs more care. Brush the burrs weekly and avoid water on them. Because the settings cluster at the coarse end, treat espresso as an occasional experiment, not a daily use.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers who want flat burrs and a proven brand.
pros: Stainless flat burrs give even particles
18 settings for drip to espresso-adjacent sizes
cons: Faster motor makes more noise and heat

products.name: SHARDOR Electric Burr Grinder 2.0, 16 Settings, Timer Dial
products.description:
SHARDOR pairs a metallic flat burr mill with sixteen micro-adjusted settings and an electric timer dial that selects between two and fourteen cups, with one-touch automatic operation and auto shut-off. The listing claims the mill grinds without burning beans.

The timer dial is a convenience, since you pick cups instead of seconds. It is a time-based dose, so the grind weight varies with bean density. Compared with the Cuisinart it adds the dial, and compared with the OXO it lacks a memory function.

Because the brand is newer, keep the receipt and check warranty terms. Clean the chute weekly. Use it with a scale and a timer on the first few mornings to learn how many seconds make your usual dose.
products.bestFor: Casual brewers who want to dial cups and walk away.
cons: Time-based dosing varies with bean density

products.name: Aromaster Conical Burr Grinder, 48 Settings, Anti-Static
products.description:
Aromaster offers 48 grind settings, stainless steel conical burrs ground evenly and slowly to reduce heat, anti-static technology and an adjustable timer up to 40 seconds. The large range runs from fine to coarse.

Step count is not the same as range, so check how the 48 steps are spread. Compared with the OXO it has more steps but a less proven design, and compared with the Baratza it offers more settings and fewer parts support.

Anti-static technology helps keep counters clean, but a drop of water on the beans also cuts static. Brush the chute weekly. The anti-static design helps, but a quick wipe of the bin after each use keeps grounds from sticking.
products.bestFor: Brewers who want many steps and an anti-static design.

products.name: Hamilton Beach Fresh Grind Electric Coffee Grinder, 12 Cups
products.description:
Hamilton Beach is a blade grinder that handles enough beans for up to twelve cups, with a dishwasher-safe grinding bowl and hideaway cord storage under the base. It also grinds spices.

Blade grinders chop beans with a spinning propeller, so particle size depends on grinding time and the mix is uneven. They suit drip and French press at a push, but they are weak for espresso and pour-over. Compared with the burr grinders in this guide it is far cheaper and simpler.

The dishwasher-safe bowl is a real convenience, and a blade grinder can double for spices, though it retains odours. Keep one unit for coffee and another for spices. Because the bowl goes in the dishwasher, it is easy to switch between coffee and spices if you rinse well.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers who brew drip coffee and want easy cleanup.
pros: Handles up to 12 cups of beans
cons: Blade grinding gives an uneven particle size

products.name: BLACK+DECKER One Touch Coffee and Spice Grinder
products.description:
This BLACK+DECKER blade grinder has stainless steel blades and bowl, a two-thirds cup capacity and a one-touch push button that sets the consistency by how long you hold it. It also grinds herbs, spices and grains.

Its compact size makes it a handy second grinder for spices. Compared with the Hamilton Beach it holds less but is smaller and easier to store, and compared with the burr grinders it is cheaper and less even.

Hold the button in short pulses and shake the unit for a more even grind. Wipe the bowl after each use. Pulse the button in short bursts and shake the unit between pulses for a more even result.
products.bestFor: Spice grinding and occasional coffee for one or two cups.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Blades chop beans and set size only by time, so particles vary widely. Burrs crush beans at a set gap, giving far more even particles. The Hamilton Beach and BLACK+DECKER are blade units, while the Baratza, OXO, Cuisinart, SHARDOR and Aromaster are burr grinders. If you brew pour-over or espresso, choose burrs. A quick way to feel the difference is to grind the same beans in a blade and a burr grinder and sift the results: the blade leaves a pile of dust and boulders, while the burr leaves a narrow band of similar pieces that extract at the same rate.

Conical burrs, as on the Baratza and OXO, run cooler and quieter. Flat burrs, as on the Cuisinart and SHARDOR, give a sharp particle distribution. Both are fine at home volumes, so choose on settings and repair support rather than shape alone. Pour-over and espresso reward fine control, while French press and drip forgive more, so rank the criteria by your most demanding brew method and let the rest fall into place.

Fifteen steps with micro-adjustments, like the OXO's 43, can cover more useful sizes than 40 coarse clicks. The Aromaster lists 48 settings, but check how they are spread. Espresso needs fine, tiny steps. If you often switch between brew methods, note where each setting sits and write the numbers on the hopper, since dialling in from scratch wastes beans.

Ground coffee stays in the chute, and stale grounds taint the next dose. Static makes grounds cling. A small brush and weekly cleaning fix retention, and a drop of water on the beans cuts static. The Aromaster adds anti-static design. Look at how ground coffee exits: a chute that is short and straight leaves less behind than a long curved one, and a removable bin makes cleaning much easier.

Blade grinders run at 80 dB or more, small burr grinders at 65 to 80 dB. Slow gear-reduction motors protect aroma, which matters for light roasts. Conical burrs on the Baratza and OXO run cooler than fast flat burrs. Heat from friction is slight at home volumes, but a slow motor protects volatile aromatics that make light roasts taste floral, so match motor speed to your roast.

A grinder used daily will eventually need burrs or a motor part. Baratza sells parts, while generic brands may not. Check before you buy, because a grinder that cannot be repaired becomes waste. Store beans in a sealed container away from light and heat, and buy a size you finish in two weeks, because even the best grinder cannot rescue stale coffee.

specDecoder.meaning: The shape of the grinding surfaces, conical or flat. Both crush beans at a fixed gap. Match the hopper size to how much you brew in a week.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Baratza and OXO use conical, and the Cuisinart and SHARDOR use flat.

specDecoder.meaning: Steps in the gap between burrs. More steps give finer control. Check how the steps are spread across the range.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Aromaster lists 48 while the Baratza has fewer.

specDecoder.meaning: Fine steps between main settings for dialling in a brew. Time-based dosing is convenient but not exact.
A time-based dose chosen by cups. It does not weigh the beans. A timer without memory means resetting each use.
specDecoder.watchFor: The SHARDOR and Aromaster use timers.

specDecoder.meaning: How many beans the container holds. Large hoppers expose beans to air. Flat and conical burrs both work well at home volumes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Grind quality design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared blade and burr designs and burr shape. Burr grinders ranked above blade units. The Baratza and OXO lead. We started from the grinding design, because a blade and a burr produce different results with the same beans.

howWeEvaluated.title: Adjustment range
howWeEvaluated.description: We read for step count and micro-adjustments. The OXO and Aromaster lead on fine control. Coarse-only ranges lose points for espresso. We compared step count against range, and we credited micro-adjustments where the listing states them.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleanup and static
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at retention, static and bowl design. The Hamilton Beach bowl is dishwasher-safe. The Aromaster adds anti-static. We looked at retention, static and bin design, since daily cleanup decides whether a grinder gets used.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered parts supply and brand support. Baratza leads for repair. Generic brands lose points. We counted parts support as part of ownership, since a grinder that can be repaired outlasts one that cannot.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each grinder to a brewer type using owner feedback patterns. The Cuisinart is the flat burr value pick, while the Baratza is the long-term pick. We kept cost to relative tiers and matched each grinder to a brewing habit.

cards.label: Blade
cards.text: The Hamilton Beach and BLACK+DECKER chop beans, so size depends on grind time. They are cheap and fine for drip.

cards.label: Burr
cards.text: The Baratza, OXO, Cuisinart, SHARDOR and Aromaster crush at a set gap for even particles. They suit pour-over and espresso.

howToChoose.note: Choose blades for budget and burrs for quality.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Burrs that give even particles, a mid-range setting with fine steps and low retention. Pour-over punishes uneven grinds with bitterness.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Baratza Encore and OXO Brew are the best fits. The Cuisinart is the value alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You brew daily and want parts and consistency. The Baratza is that grinder.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You brew drip occasionally. The Cuisinart or a blade unit does the job.

maintenance.why: Stale grounds taint the next dose and clog the path. A small paintbrush reaches the corners of the chute.
Oils build up and dull flavour. Use a stiff brush, never water. A pinch of grinder cleaning tablets can freshen burrs, though a brush is enough for most owners.
Old beans go stale and leave oils. Dry the hopper fully before refilling.
Worn burrs give uneven particles. Check the screws that hold the burr carrier.
Oils and grounds build up around the base. Keep spare parts for any wear items listed in the manual.

faq.q: Is a burr grinder worth it?
faq.a: Yes for pour-over, espresso and any brew where flavour matters. Burrs give even particles, while blades chop unevenly. Weigh your dose on a small scale, because grinders that dose by time or by cups cannot account for bean density.

faq.q: Do more grind settings mean a better grinder?
faq.a: No. Step count is not range, so a grinder with 15 steps and micro-adjustments can cover more useful sizes than 40 coarse clicks. Fresh beans from a recent roast produce more static, so a spritz of water often calms them.

faq.q: Can I grind spices in a coffee grinder?
faq.a: A blade grinder can, but it retains odours. Keep a separate unit for coffee. A grinder that rattles or smells hot is overworked or dirty, and cleaning the burrs usually fixes it.
Many years at home volumes. Replace them when particle size becomes uneven. Try your grinder's finest setting with a paper filter to see whether espresso-adjacent sizes are possible.

faq.q: Why does my grinder make a mess?
faq.a: Static makes grounds cling. A drop of water on the beans or an anti-static design cuts it. Replace the burrs when the grind feels uneven or the motor strains, since worn burrs also shave metal into the cup.

faq.q: Should I grind just before brewing?
faq.a: Yes. Whole beans keep flavour far longer than pre-ground coffee. If you only brew a cup or two at a time, a smaller hopper keeps beans fresher.
